newsitem.title: USA: Rapist Army sgt. apologizes at sentence hearing.
newsitem.headline: Rapist Army sgt. apologizes at sentence hearing.

text.p: ABERDEEN, Md., April 5 (Reuter) Army Staff Sgt. Delmar Simpson, convicted of 18 counts of rape of six trainees, apologised on Monday evening to his family, the army and the trainees he raped.
Simpson, the last of five witnesses at his sentencing hearing, admitted he failed the trainees, but did not admit the rapes.
The military jury was to begin deliberations on Tuesday morning.

Simpson, 32, was acquitted of one additional rape count last week, but found guilty of indecent assault. He also was found guilty of 25 of 35 other sexual misconduct counts against him, not guilty of seven and guilty of lesser offences on three.

The drill sergeant could face life in prison for the rape convictions. He had pleaded guilty to 11 counts of consensual sex and five counts of propositioning, for which he faced a maximum sentence of 32 years in prison.
Simpson told the six-member military court he did not understand its decision but that he accepted responsibility for his actions.

"After I started down this path, I became blind to my inability to live by the moral values I learned from childhood. I am still struggling to understand how I lost my way and am making amends to those most dear to me, my wife and my family."
He asked forgiveness from his wife, Jillette, and apologised to his 61-year-old mother, who earlier Monday evening testified on his behalf.

"I apologise to all the drill sergeants who came before me, all with whom I had the privilege of serving and most of all to all who will follow in the weeks, months and years after this trial. My actions have brought dishonour to a most honourable calling," Simpson continued.
"Finally," he said, "I apologise to the trainees who believed I brought them harm. I was your drill sergeant and I failed you as a drill sergeant."
Simpson did not testify at the trial, but his defence maintained that sex with trainees was consensual.

Earlier, a forensic psychiatrist from Walter Reed military hospital in Washington testified that Simpson suffered from a narcissistic personality disorder but was able to distinguish right from wrong.
Dr. Raymond Lande, testifying for the defence, said the disorder involved Simpson weighing risks against rewards and taking advantage of others to attain the rewards.
If Simpson were sentenced to more than a year in jail or discharged from the service for bad conduct, the case would automatically go to the Army's Court of Criminal Appeals.

If the Army court of appeals upheld the verdict, then Simpson could appeal to the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Armed Forces. If that court did not take the case, then Simpson could go to the U.S. Supreme Court.
Simpson was the first of 12 trainers charged with various acts of misconduct at Aberdeen to go before a court-martial and was charged with the most rapes.
